title: Line up two bearings with a motor's shaft
instruction: Line up the two bearings with the motor's shaft: set one about 10 cm and one about 20 cm out from the motor's front face, each centred on the shaft's line and square to it, so a straight shaft would pass through both.
context: Before a drive shaft goes in, the bearings that carry it are set in line with the motor's shaft; a bearing off the line or turned binds the shaft and wears out. Only a short stub of the motor's shaft shows, so its line has to be carried out by eye to where each bearing goes, and each bearing turned square to it. Done by: millwrights and industrial machinery mechanics.
setup: Positions are in cm on the table, from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left; turns are anticlockwise seen from above, from straight out. A dark grey electric motor (10 cm long, 6 cm wide, 5 cm tall) is fixed with its centre at (13.7, 12.3), turned 30 degrees, with an orange shaft stub (1.8 x 1.8 cm, 3 cm long) sticking out of the centre of its front face, at (18.0, 14.8), 2.5 cm above the table. Two blue pillow-block bearings with hollow cast housings (3 cm thick, 6 cm wide, 5 cm tall, 200 g; the bore runs through the 3 cm thickness, 2.5 cm up) stand on the table: one centred at (23, 30), turned 10 degrees, and one at (36, 33), turned 55 degrees. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The shaft's line runs from the stub straight out along the motor's axis, 2.5 cm above the table. A bearing is standing when its base is within 5 degrees of flat and its lowest point within 3 mm of the table, and still when it moves under 1 cm/s and turns under 0.5 rad/s. It is in line when it is standing and still with its centre within 3 mm of the shaft's line and its bore within 2 degrees of square to it; roughly in line within 10 mm and 6 degrees. There are two places along the shaft, 8 to 12 cm and 18 to 22 cm out from the motor's front face, and either bearing can go in either. Each place scores 0.5 if a bearing is in line there and 0.25 if roughly in line; the two bearings are matched to the two places whichever way scores more, and one bearing can't earn both. Both in line: 1.0, if the line through the two bearings' centres is also within 1 degree of the shaft, so that a straight shaft through both bores would meet the motor's; otherwise 0.75. If a bearing ends off the table (its lowest point more than 1 cm below the table top), the score is 0.
reset_notes: Stand the two bearings back at their marks, turned 10 and 55 degrees.
fidelity: The bearings are solid blocks with no bore and no shaft is fitted: the score checks each block's centre line against the motor's axis. Height needs no setting, since the bores are at shaft height on a flat table. Real millwrights align to hundredths of a millimetre with shims and indicators; this asks for 3 mm and 2 degrees. Every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic).
